title: Input direction improved spatial stimulus prediction, but overall task gains depended on geometry, in 176 IBL regions
abstract: We tested whether directed input fingerprints improve held-region task prediction over output and undirected fingerprints. We used 176 IBL regions, the Knox connectome and Allen MERFISH composition. Nested ridge prediction used matched random, spatial and 0.5 mm buffered spatial folds, with three geometry reference lengths. Input had lower mean task error than output fingerprints in all nine settings. Against undirected fingerprints, the spatial task ranking changed with the geometry reference. At 1 mm, undirected wiring retained 93.0 percent of the input error reduction in spatial folds and 96.8 percent with a buffer. Input gave lower mean stimulus error in every setting; undirected wiring gave lower feedback and block-prior errors in both spatial designs at all three geometry lengths. The fixed mean input/output kernel gave small intrinsic prediction gains over input alone in both spatial designs. Repeat ranges reuse the same regions and are not confidence intervals. These are prediction results in one existing cohort. They do not divide causal control between wiring and cell types. Code, input hashes, aggregate scores, figures and external regeneration steps are supplied. External records and derived regional matrices are not bundled.
